prompt: A 10 Gbit/s link is flooded with minimum-size Ethernet frames (84 bytes on the wire including preamble and gap). About how much time does the receiver have per packet to keep up?

options.explanation: Correct. 84 bytes is 672 bits; at 10 billion bits per second that is about 14.88 million packets per second, or one every 67 ns.
That's the budget at 100 Gbit/s, ten times faster.
Far too generous: that's 100 times the real budget, roughly what a 100 Mbit/s link gives you.

workedExample:
Using the supplied occupancy model:

```formula
L = 84 B × 8 bit/B = 672 bit
T = L / C
T = (672 bit) / (10^10 bit/s)
T = 6.72 × 10^−8 s = 67.2 ns
P = 1 / T ≈ 14.88 × 10^6 /s
where
L: wire occupancy of one minimum frame, in bits
C: link rate, 10 Gbit/s = 10^10 bit/s
T: time between back-to-back frames
P: maximum frames per second
B: byte; bit/B means 8 bits per byte
bit: binary digit, the unit of data
s: second; "/s" means per second
ns: nanosecond, 10^−9 s
≈: approximately equal to
In words: each minimum frame occupies 672 bit-times, which at 10 Gbit/s is 67.2 ns, about 14.88 million frames a second.
```
 This is aggregate arrival spacing; memory-level parallelism, batching, offloads and multiple cores determine processing capacity. No fixed DRAM/syscall latency is implied.
